questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer:
It was crucial for me to go to a destination far away from home, but still in a culture that would be easy for me to live in. Personally, I wanted to see something entirely different from Denmark, but still be in a place where people spoke English, so it would be easy to get to know people where I went. 
I also enjoyed the weather a lot compared to home... And the beautiful nature of course. 

Academically, it was important to me to go to an English-speaking country, as my guess was I would learn more there than in a non-English-speaking country. Furthermore, I wanted to go to a uni with high academic standards and interesting courses.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer:
There was an orientation meeting for all exchange students at the beginning of the semester, which was helpful to go to. Other than that, my host uni was hard to get into contact with, I feel like. 
They were slow at responding to e-mails, and their websites and systems were hard to figure out. I got some help from my fellow Danish exchange students, but it was clear that the exchange team at the host uni was very busy.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: There was an orientation meeting for all exchange students at the beginning of the semester, which was helpful to go to. I also received some e-mails from the host uni, but the amount of information was so overwhelming that it had the opposite effect. It was very hard to know which information was nice to know, and which was need to know.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I was very very lucky and found a townhouse with three of my uni friends from home. We found it a couple of months before we left for exchange on a Facebook page called "Young Danes in Sydney". But most people would not recommend finding housing off campus before you're there, as there are many people trying to scam you. But in general, Facebook is a good place to look for housing. There are plenty of pages where you can search for housing.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: It's really really expensive. I paid over 7000 DKK in rent a month to stay in a house where we had ants, snails, cockroaches, and a rat. There's a housing crisis in Sydney, and it's not going away. It can also be hard to find a place if you don't have one before you go, but many people do it - often with someone they found at uni which is nice.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: The registration process was long and infuriating. First, you have to apply for courses in a system called Endeavour. UNSW will then approve or decline your courses there. You need to apply for as many courses as you can, as it is better to have a lot of "pre-approved" courses. Afterwards, you have to apply again for the courses in their student system called myUNSW. It was a long, hard process, as UNSW had very limited spaces for students in their law classes. I got rejected for many courses before finally getting some of the ones I wanted, so you have to be very patient in the process and accept the fact that you might not get all the courses you want.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: There is an exchange team at UNSW who helped me. They were helpful ones you finally got a hold of them, but bad at replying for the most part.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: In the end, I actually got some nice courses that didn't collide with each other. But it was a long way coming and took some time after I got there.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Have patience. Don't stress that you don't have all of it figured out before you go. Course registration can be done even after you've started classes, even though it's of course nice to have figured out before. I think I had my final registration done about a week before I started classes.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The level of courses was a bit easier than at home, but harder to follow because of the language barrier. Both the BA and MA courses were, in my opinion, easier to pass than at UCPH.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
The style of teaching in Australia is very different from Denmark. First of all, you don't just get graded on a final exam. Your participation in classes gets grated, and you often have quizzes and research papers during the semester which also get graded. Classes are compulsory to be at. 
You have to state your own opinion - both in class and in your written assignments. That's a whole other way to learn than at UCPH. It has its ups and downs - depending on who you are. I thought it was nice with a change, but also a bit harder during the semester to keep up with your assignments and the quizzes and also concentrate on participating in class.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
LAWS3623 - The Criminal Trial
LAWS8058 - Managing Workplace Change and Conflict
LAWS8168 - The Australian Legal System in Comparative Perspective
CRIM1011 - Introduction to Criminal Justice

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: All of my courses were nice, and very different from one another. The Criminal Trial was nice, the teacher was very sweet and interested in the Danish legal system. She also arranged for me to see an Australian criminal trial, which was very interesting. The Australian Legal System in Comparative Perspective is made for law exchange students and was a nice way to get an introduction to how their legal system and laws work. It's a very intensive course with a lot of studying though.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer:
I was not expecting to travel around Australia as much as I did. I took lots more trips outside Sydney as I did expect. So did everyone else. Save up to go travel as well while you're there. 

You want to experience the city as well, so it's nice to have money to have drinks and go out to eat from time to time.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
The cost of living is expensive. Food was expensive, alcohol was expensive, and housing was very expensive. Our gas and water bill was also very much more expensive than I'd thought. Flights to and from DK are very expensive as well

Avocados and coffee is cheap and good :)

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: I did not look into it that much, but there were a lot of activities to participate in. There is also a gym and a pool at campus.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I did not participate in any, as I did not feel like I had the time.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Definitely go to Byron Bay and Melbourne for long weekends. Drive the great ocean road in Melbourne. Surf on Bondi Beach on your weekends. Go for at least two weeks to Western Australia in a camper van - most amazing vacation of my life. I stopped for two weeks in Bali on my way home. I would also recommend doing that.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It was very easy, I feel like. Australia has a very western culture like Denmark.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Australians are very open. Talk to them in class :)

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer:
I didn't find the big cultural differences with Australians, other than they're all really fascinated by the fact that you've traveled a lot. 
There are a lot of Chinese students in Australia, and I felt the social distance to them was big. They're not unfriendly, but they keep a lot to themselves, and it can be hard to socialise. There is also just a big cultural difference and language barrier, which is hard to overcome.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I appreciated the nature a lot. Although Sydney is a big city, their nature is still unbelievably beautiful.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1) Studying there is not a piece of cake. Although it is easier to pass courses, they read twice as much as we do at UCPH. It is more busy during the semester, but I chose courses without final exams, so I didn't have an "exam-period" per se, which was nice. 

2) Be patient in your communication with the uni. 

3) Be open-minded in your choice of courses. You're not guaranteed all the courses you want.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: I had a friend who had been at the same uni the year before me. It was really nice to have a person to ask questions.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Getting to know a lot of new people, learning about an entirely different legal system, and seeing places I would never had imagined seeing in my lifetime.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: I didn't expect it to be that hard to study in English - but it was. Although I'm pretty good at English, academically it is challenging to keep up. Everything takes twice as long to read, and twice as long to write.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
